title: Children’s social care: gaps, illegal homes and why data and joined-up services matter
label: 11 November 2026 · Children’s social care evidence session
summary: Dame Rachel de Souza, Children’s Commissioner for England, told the committee that the children’s social care system is failing many children—especially those with complex needs—pointing to illegal unregistered homes, poor outcomes in education and justice, weak delivery of reforms, and poor data sharing. She recommended clearer accountability, faster registration and inspection, a national unique identifier for children, properly planned local capacity, stronger family support, and action to stop profit-making that harms children.

glossary.definition: The government inspectorate for education and children’s social care in England.
Care Quality Commission — the regulator for health and adult social care services in England, including some specialist children’s services.
The main law setting out duties for children’s social care; Dame Rachel says it needs updating for modern risks.
Proposed groupings of services and councils to plan and share specialist placements for children across an area.
A single identifier for each child that would let health, education, social care and justice share relevant records safely.
The duty on local authorities and public bodies to act like a responsible parent for children in their care.
When a young person is held in custody while awaiting trial or further court decisions.
Young Offender Institution — a prison for young people.
Deprivation of liberty — legal authorisation for restricting a person's freedom for their own safety.

chapters.title: The overall picture: failing too many children
chapters.takeaway: Dame Rachel says children’s social care still fails many children—high-profile tragedies and quieter, widespread harms show the system is not delivering.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Dame Rachel, to start: is the children’s social care system meeting needs and delivering good outcomes, especially for children with complex needs or deprived of their liberty?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: No. There are high-profile avoidable deaths and many quieter failures. Children are in illegal homes, education outcomes are poor, care leavers face homelessness, and we have children stuck in hospital or prison because services do not join up.

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: I published a large set of child metrics called 'Childhood Lottery' showing huge variation by area: some places do much worse on placements, social worker turnover and support for care leavers.

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: I’m frustrated that many so-called reforms are ideas on paper without delivery. The system needs stronger accountability, data and focused action.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mentioned prisons and mental health provision—do you work closely with the CQC on specialist mental health services for children?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: There are good people in both inspectorates, but we need Ofsted and CQC to work much more closely with social care so specialist provision is planned before children are placed there.

chapters.title: Illegal, unregistered homes: scale, cost and solutions
chapters.takeaway: About 669 children are in unregistered homes; Dame Rachel calls the practice illegal, expensive and avoidable, and demands faster registration and local planning.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Chittlehampton
turns.text: You said 669 children were in illegal homes and it cost £350 million last year. Why is this happening and what should the DfE do?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: It’s partly lack of capacity and poor planning. But illegal is illegal: councils and Ofsted should not pass inspections if children are placed in illegal homes. Registration delays must be fixed and areas must plan five-year strategies for beds and specialist foster care.

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Some placements cost £10,000 a week or even £1 million a year for individual children, often in caravans or B&Bs. That money could be used to build proper local provision or support families.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Chittlehampton
turns.text: Directors say they have to use illegal placements at short notice. You’re saying they should have planned for that before the crisis?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Yes. Strategic planning and sufficiency of local placements are practical and doable. If each MP took one child from the backlog, it would show how small numbers actually are—this is solvable.

turns.speaker: Baroness Watkins of Tavistock
turns.text: Some local authorities have ready homes but can’t get Ofsted to inspect them quickly. Could councils inspect each other or use a neutral body?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: I’m open to pragmatic solutions, but beware unintended consequences. The DfE used to register free schools and had capacity; a neutral, trusted route for quicker sign-off could help if it’s done carefully.

chapters.title: Inspection, profit and the role of regulators
chapters.takeaway: Dame Rachel welcomes Ofsted action on illegal homes but criticises slow registration, widespread private-profit provision and asks for clearer inspection standards.

turns.speaker: Lord Mohammed of Tinsley
turns.text: Ofsted may grade a home as 'good' yet outcomes for looked-after children remain poor. How do we fix that?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Ofsted’s new framework could help if it focuses on outcomes, inclusion and stops accepting minimum standards. Inspectors need the courage to draw lines—particularly over illegal placements.

turns.speaker: Lord Mohammed of Tinsley
turns.text: Should registration and inspection be separated? Do current Ofsted responsibilities cause a problem?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Separation can work: schools were registered by DfE and inspected by Ofsted. The immediate problem is delays in registering homes—hurry up and register them and don’t accept illegal placements.

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Another issue is private profit. A small number of companies run most children’s homes and have made large profits. I don’t think profit should be driving placements where children are vulnerable.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Chittlehampton
turns.text: You used to run schools—how do you see regulation here compared with education reforms?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Education has shown reform can work with clear accountability and data. Children’s social care needs the same focus, and regulators must use data and standards to drive change.

chapters.title: Data, unique ID and joined-up services
chapters.takeaway: Dame Rachel argues a national unique identifier and better data sharing between health, education, social care and justice would prevent children from slipping through the gaps.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Chittlehampton
turns.text: You keep returning to unique IDs and data systems. Should creating that be a top recommendation?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Yes. A single identifier would let professionals see a child’s whole history and stop repeated missed opportunities—Prevent referrals, hospital stays, or children off school who aren’t known to services.

turns.speaker: Baroness Nichols of Selby
turns.text: People hide behind data protection. Why can’t agencies share data that would protect children?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Many are allowed to share but lack the systems and courage. Local examples show police or health teams find children not on any roll. A digitised 'red book' for each child, with safeguards, would transform care.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could the single patient record in the Health Bill be the vehicle for progress on a child unique ID?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Possibly. If social care can’t lead, health could, but it must be multi-agency and include justice. The goal is joined-up records for children across services.

chapters.title: Prevention, fostering, regional planning and next steps
chapters.takeaway: She urges more family support, clearer foster recruitment messaging, regional planning for specialist placements, five-year strategies and true corporate parenting.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hollins
turns.text: Could regional care co-operatives help supply placements and move children out of secure or long-stay psychiatric care?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: They have big potential to plan and pool specialist beds and support families, but so far they’re mostly paper ideas. We must align footprints—health, education and local government—and deliver, not just pilot.

turns.speaker: Baroness Redfern
turns.text: You welcomed powers to cap profit. How would that work?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: In principle I’d avoid profit-making in placements and instead grow social enterprises and proper local provision. The law must be clear about what profits, if any, are acceptable and how to enforce caps.

turns.speaker: Baroness Nichols of Selby
turns.text: Fostering is short of carers. Why don’t people foster now?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Many prospective carers are put off early by clumsy processes or being asked about finances first. Most children needing foster care today have complex needs. Recruitment needs a better public campaign and clearer step-in expectations and support.

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Prevention matters: family hubs, early years and school-centred support work where they’re properly funded. We can avoid many care entries with sustained local family help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final question: what are the top practical steps you want to see now?

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: First, stop using illegal homes and speed up registration; second, plan capacity with five-year strategies and regional co-ops; third, create a functioning unique ID and shared records; fourth, back family support and foster recruitment; and fifth, insist on true corporate parenting across services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Your evidence has been clear and pressing. We appreciate your work and time today.

turns.speaker: Dame Rachel de Souza
turns.text: Thank you. I will share more specific numbers on things like long-term isolation on wards, and I’m happy to keep working with the committee.
